unitDescription.value: In this unit, students investigate the intersection of food specialisations and emerging technologies through the application of virtual reality (VR) in culinary contexts. Students explore how immersive digital environments can simulate kitchen safety, complex culinary techniques, and production workflows to improve efficiency and reduce resource waste. They examine the role of simulation in modern food industries, considering how virtual environments support skill development and ethical decision-making in high-risk or resource-intensive scenarios. Through the design process, students generate and represent original ideas for virtual cooking experiences, using graphical representation techniques and storyboards to communicate their design thinking. The unit emphasises innovation, user experience, and the strategic use of technologies to address contemporary challenges in food production and training for preferred futures.

description.value: In this design project, students investigate contemporary drivers of food trends to define a design opportunity within a professional culinary context. Students select a specific driver—such as sustainability, health and wellbeing, or cultural fusion—to guide the development of a designed solution. They apply divergent design thinking to generate and explore multiple concepts, evaluated against specific criteria: trend alignment, environmental sustainability, and aesthetic appearance. Through iterative refinement and the use of graphical representation techniques, students communicate a final dish design, justifying their decisions based on technical, environmental, and social factors. The production phase utilises virtual reality (VR) technology to simulate complex culinary workflows, allowing students to demonstrate production skills and manage safety and efficiency in a digital environment. Finally, students evaluate the success of their designed solution and the effectiveness of the virtual production process against the established design criteria.
description.aiNotes:
Task 1 – Identify the Driver (Define) 

Choose one modern driver of food trends to guide your design. 
Examples: 

Health and wellbeing (e.g. high-protein, low-sugar, plant-based) 

Environmental sustainability (e.g. local produce, minimal waste) 

Cultural fusion (e.g. mixing flavours or ingredients from different cultures) 

Convenience and lifestyle (e.g. meals for busy people, easy to prepare) 

Deliverable: 

A short paragraph explaining your chosen food trend driver 

 

Task 2 – Generate Ideas (Develop) 

Use divergent thinking to explore a wide range of ideas. 

Focus on one design criterion at a time. The 3 criteria are trend alignment, sustainability, appearance 

Create at least five different ideas for each criterion 

Use sketches, notes, or diagrams to show your thinking 

Deliverable: 

A3 page showing idea generation and exploration (sketches, annotations, mind maps) 

 

Task 3 – Combine and Refine 

Narrow down and improve your ideas. 

Combine your best elements into 2–3 refined concepts 

Justify why each concept could work for the restaurant 

Evaluate against the criteria to see which one best suits 

Deliverable: 

A3 page showing refined ideas with annotations and justifications 

 

Task 4 – Final Design (Deliver) 

Present your final dish design. 

Clearly show what the dish looks like (drawings, photos, or digital visuals) 

Explain how it reflects your chosen food trend driver 

Describe how it meets all three criteria 

Deliverable: 

A3 page showing your final concept with clear visuals and explanations 

 

Task 5 – Cook it in VR 

Create a video of you cooking a representation of the dish in VR.  

Evaluate how well your dish meets each design criterion 

Deliverable: 

Cooking video presentation

They communicate design ideas, processes and solutions to a range of audiences, including using digital tools. activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through the physical and software calibration routine step by step. Model: 1. Adjusting rear strap tension. 2. - Guardian boundary: Clear of desks, chairs, and neighbouring students.
- Floor plane: Virtual grid sits flush on physical floor.
- Audio balance: Able to hear virtual cues while still hearing teacher voice.

activities.title: Deconstructing Controller Haptics
activities.teacherDoes: Project a detailed diagram of the VR handheld controller. Model the 4 functional inputs: 'Notice Callout 1: Index Trigger provides variable pull resistance for delicate actions like picking up a raspberry. Callout 2: Grip Button activates the full palm squeeze for gripping heavy chef knives and saucepans. Callout 3: Primary Thumbstick manages snap-turning. Callout 4: Haptic Vibration Motor pulses when virtual metal contacts a cutting board.'
activities.studentsDo: Examine the projected controller schematic. On the annotate diagram in the workbook, write the functional role and haptic response type for each of the 4 callouts.
activities.visibleInstructions: Annotate the 4 numbered callouts on your VR controller diagram. For each callout, write the input name, its culinary action (e.g. grip knife), and the haptic feedback type.
activities.questioning:
q: Why is varying vibration duration used to simulate object weight in VR when the controller itself does not change mass?
Expected: The brain integrates auditory and haptic pulses to infer mass and density through sensory substitution.
q: What design problem arises if the grip button requires too much continuous squeeze pressure?
Expected: User fatigue, cramping, and unintentional dropping of virtual items during prolonged food preparation.
activities.scaffolding:
Callout Bank:
1. Index Trigger: Squeeze sensitivity for precision pinch and delicate garnishes (light tap haptic).
2. Grip Button: Palm squeeze for grasping knives, pans, and large tools (sustained rumble).
3. Primary Thumbstick: Directional push for snap-rotation and teleportation (click feedback).
4. Haptic Vibration Motor: Internal motor delivering collision cues when cutting or placing objects.

activities.teacherDoes: Model evaluating VR interaction fidelity: 'I rate my first trial at 3.5 out of 5. While my knife grip was solid, collision clipping on the onion caused one slice to fly off the board, demonstrating where simulation physics differs from reality.' Instruct students to rate their procedural efficiency and write a 2-sentence technical justification.
activities.studentsDo: Plot their operational efficiency score on the 1–5 continuum and write a 2-sentence justification citing specific physics or controller friction points (e.g. tracking latency, trigger sensitivity, clipping).
activities.visibleInstructions: Mark your efficiency score on the 1 to 5 scale. Below the scale, write 2 sentences justifying your score using at least one technical term (e.g. haptic lag, collision boundary, trigger response).
activities.questioning: What specific adjustment to collision boundaries would make virtual food preparation feel more natural? Expected: Tightening mesh boundaries so small ingredients cannot slip through the cutting board or knife blade. How does tracking your virtual efficiency inform sustainable food design? Expected: It highlights ergonomic bottlenecks and procedural mistakes before purchasing expensive commercial ingredients or machinery.
activities.scaffolding:
Continuum scale anchors: 1 = Severe interaction friction (dropped tools, dropped ingredients, disorientation); 3 = Moderate control (successful dish with minor clipping or delayed slicing); 5 = Flawless efficiency (fluid knife handling, accurate thermal transfer, zero wasted motion).
Key terms: Collision mesh, tracking latency, haptic pulse, snap-turn, boundary drift.

activities.title: Food Safety and HACCP Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the four foundational food safety concepts: Cross-contamination, Temperature Danger Zone (5°C–60°C), High-Risk Foods, and HACCP (Hazard Analysis Critical Control Points). Model the application of these concepts in a commercial kitchen context: 'For example, if we use a red board for raw beef, we prevent cross-contamination by ensuring that specific surface does not touch ready-to-eat salad items. Similarly, a HACCP plan requires us to record temperatures, ensuring proteins never linger in the Temperature Danger Zone where binary fission causes bacterial populations to double every 20 minutes.'
activities.studentsDo: Students will engage with the 'Food Safety Vocabulary' activity to reinforce key industry terminology required for safe kitchen operation. Students select the appropriate definition from the provided bank and match it to the corresponding industry term in the table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using the definitions provided in the bank below, match the term to the correct industry definition. Write the full definition in the Match column corresponding to each industry term.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must raw poultry and cooked meats be physically separated using colour-coded equipment?
expected: To prevent cross-contamination, ensuring harmful pathogens like Salmonella or Campylobacter are not transferred from raw proteins to ready-to-eat consumables.
question: What is the critical significance of the 5°C to 60°C range in HACCP protocols?
expected: This is the Temperature Danger Zone where bacterial growth is most rapid; keeping food outside this range is a primary critical control point for preventing foodborne illness.
activities.scaffolding: Definitions: Cross-contamination (the transfer of harmful microorganisms from raw food or surfaces to cooked/ready food). HACCP (a systematic preventive approach to food safety from biological, chemical, and physical hazards). Temperature Danger Zone (the 5°C–60°C range where food poisoning bacteria multiply most rapidly). High-Risk Foods (foods rich in protein and moisture, e.g., dairy, poultry, seafood, that support rapid microbial growth).
activities.eLearning: Display the St Brendan's College digital food safety resource centre or relevant industry standard diagrams on the smartboard. Ensure students access the VR kitchen environment only after completing this vocabulary task.
activities.transition: Now that we have locked in our key safety definitions, let's trace how these critical control points are established across actual food preparation workflows within our VR simulation.

activities.title: HACCP Critical Control Points
activities.teacherDoes: Deliver a brief briefing on the three HACCP phases: Receiving, Prepping, and Cooking. Model the identification of a Critical Control Point (CCP) using a whiteboard scenario: 'When prepping chicken, what is our critical limit?' Demonstrate how digital logging platforms automate these checks. Provide the scaffolded definitions for 'Critical Limit' (the maximum or minimum value to which a biological, chemical, or physical parameter must be controlled) and 'Sanitisation' (the process of reducing microorganisms to a safe level).
activities.studentsDo: Engage with the guided notes to establish technical vocabulary. Students define the parameters of a critical control point during the preparation of high-risk items like poultry. Students then complete the four-part cloze passage to formalise their understanding of HACCP compliance.
activities.visibleInstructions: Using the provided word bank, complete the sentences in your workbook to define HACCP operational standards for kitchen safety.
activities.questioning:
question: How does digital logging of critical control points assist a head chef in maintaining compliance?
expected: It creates a verifiable, timestamped audit trail that prevents human error and allows for immediate identification of temperature violations.
question: Why is the cooking stage critical control point set at 75°C core temperature?
expected: 75°C is the standard threshold to destroy vegetative pathogenic bacteria like Listeria and Salmonella, ensuring the product is safe for consumption.
activities.scaffolding: Definition 1: Critical Limit: The maximum or minimum value to which a biological, chemical, or physical parameter must be controlled at a CCP to prevent, eliminate, or reduce to an acceptable level the occurrence of a food safety hazard. Definition 2: Sanitisation: The process of reducing the number of microorganisms to a safe level using heat or chemical agents.

activities.visibleInstructions: Using the overlap table, classify safety elements into Physical Only, Shared Protocols (Both), or VR Simulation Only. Ensure you identify at least two unique constraints for each column.
activities.questioning: How does the ability to 'reset' a simulation enhance the mastery of HACCP principles? activities.scaffolding: Safety Protocols (Shared): HACCP temperature logging, handwashing frequency, sanitising food contact surfaces. Board: click 'Select Board' and choose green (vegetables). 3. Prep: hold 'Grab' on the vegetable, move to board, execute 5mm uniform cuts using the 'Claw Grip' VR controller mode. 4. activities.questioning:
Why must prep bowls be positioned on the non-dominant side before beginning slicing? Expected: It establishes a clean left-to-right workflow that prevents knife collisions and accidental cross-contact.
How does VR knife angle adjustment simulate physical claw-grip knife safety? Expected: It enforces proper controller tilt and steady downward slicing motions rather than rapid erratic hacking.

activities.teacherDoes: Project the VR cooktop interface. Model the process: 'When I initiate the sauté sequence, I first rotate the digital dial to 160°C. Notice the HUD thermal bar; I am looking for the visual cue of the Maillard reaction. If the bar enters the red zone, I demonstrate the 'thermal recovery' action—lifting the pan to break the heat source contact, preventing the digital food asset from charring. Emphasize that efficient workflow relies on monitoring these HUD elements while prepping the next ingredient.'
activities.studentsDo: Follow the teacher's VR screen projection. Map the interface components onto the provided wireframe stencil, specifically delineating where thermal data is displayed versus where physical interaction occurs.

activities.questioning: What visual cues in the simulation indicate a pan has exceeded the smoke point for oil? Expected: Rapid dark grey vapour particles and an amber flashing warning on the station HUD. Why is burner pre-heating essential before adding protein? Expected: To immediately initiate surface searing (Maillard reaction) and prevent protein from soaking in oil at low temperatures.

activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the 'Dual-Process' monitoring technique via projector. Model the verbal protocol for the Navigator: 'Temp rising, check thermostat, adjust burner down'. Provide a live exemplar using the VR interface showing how to adjust Burner A (boil) while simultaneously monitoring the viscosity and temperature of a reduction on Burner B (simmer). Emphasize that efficient workflow relies on synchronized communication to prevent heat overshoot.
activities.studentsDo: In pairs, the 'Driver' executes dual-burner temperature adjustments in the VR environment. The 'Navigator' tracks the time-to-temperature and heat milestones, recording them into the workbook to ensure procedural adherence to the recipe's thermal requirements.

Expected: The sauce reached 98°C and risked scorching, requiring power reduction to maintain a 85°C simmer. Driver, how do you prevent boil-over when adding cold prep into boiling water? Expected: Maintain burner output on high until temperature recovers, then dial back once rolling boil resumes.
activities.scaffolding:
Thermal control definitions: 
1. Thermal Inertia: The delay in temperature change after adjusting heat input.
2. Boil-over: Rapid temperature spike causing liquid expansion past vessel capacity.
3. Simmering: Maintaining a temperature between 85°C–95°C without vigorous agitation.

question: What made staging the vegetable additions based on density critical during this stir-fry?
expected: Dense root vegetables (carrots) require longer cooking time than tender capsicum to reach identical doneness simultaneously; incorrect staging leads to textural failure.
question: How did you know the protein was ready for sauce integration?

5. Deglaze and simmer sauce (1 minute reduction).
Thermal Logic: Maillard reaction (140°C-165°C) is key to flavour; avoid exceeding 185°C to prevent carbonisation.

activities.title: Defining Macro Food Trend Drivers
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly distinguish macro trend drivers from transient fads. Delivery script: 'To design viable culinary solutions, designers must separate fleeting viral fads—like butter boards—from structural trend drivers. A macro driver reflects permanent shifts in technology, resource availability, consumer health, or ethics. For example, Environmental Sustainability is a direct response to carbon reduction mandates and packaging regulations, forcing kitchens into circular waste management. Health and Wellbeing addresses physiological requirements and nutrient density.' Rear-of-room monitoring during completion.

activities.visibleInstructions: Review the four macro trend drivers. Match each term to its correct definition from the definition bank by writing the matching letter in the blank column.
activities.questioning:
Why is a structural trend driver more valuable to a culinary designer than a viral food fad? Expected: A trend driver reflects permanent consumer needs, regulatory shifts, and economic forces, ensuring product longevity, whereas fads disappear quickly.
How does the health and wellbeing driver alter professional menu development beyond simple calorie reduction? Expected: It requires nutrient-dense formulations, clean labels, functional bio-available ingredients, and verified allergen management.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Macro Trend Driver: A sustained, structural force in society, technology, or the environment that reshapes long-term consumer demand.
- Transient Fad: A temporary spike in product popularity driven by novelty or social media virality with no lasting supply chain impact.
- Environmental Sustainability: Design focused on reduced carbon footprints, circular resource management, and biodegradable materials.
- Health and Wellbeing: Design targeting physiological nourishment, functional nutrition, and specific dietary needs.
- Ethical and Cultural Fusion: Design integrating fair-trade supply chains, cultural heritage, and plant-based alternatives.
- Aesthetic Culture: Design driven by visual storytelling, sensory plating, and digital media engagement.

activities.title: Science of Spoilage and Preservation Mechanisms
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly explain the key biochemical drivers of food degradation: enzymatic browning, microbial proliferation, and moisture-driven autolysis. Model how preservation methods manipulate these mechanisms: 'Dehydration eliminates unbound water activity (aw), denying bacteria the medium needed to metabolise. Pickling lowers the solution pH below 4.6, denaturing microbial proteins.' Direct students to complete the vocabulary match in their workbooks.
activities.studentsDo: Review the four preservation and spoilage terms. Read the definition bank and write the correct matching letter or definition next to each term in the workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each preservation or spoilage term in your workbook table with its accurate scientific description from the bank.
activities.questioning:
Why does lowering water activity (aw) below 0.60 halt microbial reproduction? Expected: Microorganisms require free water for cellular transport and enzymatic processes; without free water, microbial cells become dormant or desiccate.
How does introducing acetic acid in pickling prevent food-borne pathogens like Clostridium botulinum from germinating? Expected: The acidic pH below 4.6 disrupts trans-membrane electrical potential and denatures essential microbial enzymes, arresting growth.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
- Enzymatic Browning: An oxidation reaction where polyphenol oxidase enzymes catalyse phenols into brown pigments in the presence of oxygen.
- Microbial Spoilage: Cellular deterioration caused by the exponential growth of bacteria, moulds, or yeasts metabolising nutrients.
- Acid Pickling: Chemical preservation where foods are submerged in an acidic brine (pH < 4.6) to inhibit microbial enzyme activity.
- Dehydration: Physical preservation involving heat or forced ventilation to lower water activity (aw) below microbial survival thresholds.

activities.title: Unpacking Design Brief Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the foundational vocabulary of design briefs aligned with QCAA Food & Hospitality standards. Model the difference between client needs, trend drivers, and constraints using Keppel Bay Marina's hospitality operations in Yeppoon as a case study. Model how a strict ingredient budget of $6.50 per serve is a quantitative constraint, while highlighting local seafood provenance is a response to a regional sustainability trend driver.

activities.questioning:
prompt: Why is Keppel Bay Marina's commitment to local seafood classified as both a client need and a constraint?
expected: It is a client need because it defines brand identity and consumer expectation, and a constraint because it limits ingredient procurement strictly to local fisheries within the Capricorn Coast region.
prompt: How does a design constraint differ fundamentally from a project goal?
expected: A goal is a desired aspirational outcome or target, whereas a constraint is a non-negotiable limitation or boundary parameter that the final food solution must strictly adhere to.
activities.scaffolding: Design Brief: A structured document outlining the problem, context, parameters, and criteria for a design solution. Constraint: A non-negotiable parameter or limitation such as budget, equipment, allergens, or preparation time. Trend Driver: A broader societal, environmental, or cultural shift (e.g. sustainability, local provenance) influencing consumer expectations.

lessons.title: Establishing Criteria for Success
lessons.learningGoal: Establish qualitative and quantitative criteria for success to define measurable design outcomes.

orientate.smartStart: Students complete a 5-minute classification task in their workbooks, categorizing six given product statements as either 'Qualitative' (sensory/descriptive) or 'Quantitative' (numerical/metric-based).

activities.title: Classifying Qualitative vs Quantitative Metrics
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly model how to distinguish between qualitative and quantitative criteria in food design. Demonstrate how vague goals ('make it taste good' or 'make it healthy') fail QCAA assessment standards, and show how to convert them into measurable standards (e.g., 'Score ≥4/5 on a 5-point sensory Likert scale for crispness' vs 'Provide ≥20g of protein and ≤5g of saturated fat per serving'). Model the first row on the board, showing students how to write 'Quantitative' and specify 'Digital stopwatch / minutes' as the verification tool.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the criteria classification and measurement audit table in their workbooks, identifying whether each provided criterion is qualitative or quantitative and naming its specific verification tool or unit.
activities.visibleInstructions: In your workbook table, classify each design criterion as Qualitative or Quantitative, then record the specific measurement tool or unit used to evaluate it.
activities.questioning:
prompt: Why is 'the dish must look attractive' an invalid design criterion on its own for QCAA assessment?
expected: It is subjective and cannot be objectively verified; it needs an explicit visual standard or structured rubric score.
prompt: What makes carbon footprint or food miles an effective quantitative criterion?
expected: It can be calculated and verified in exact numerical units (e.g. kilometres travelled or grams of CO2 equivalent).
activities.scaffolding: Qualitative: Sensory, descriptive, or aesthetic properties (evaluated via sensory ballots, hedonic scales, appearance rubrics). Quantitative: Numerical, measurable values (evaluated via scales, timers, nutritional databases, costing sheets).
activities.eLearning: Laptops closed; direct instruction followed by individual workbook audit.
activities.transition: Now that we can classify criteria, let's co-construct a set of balanced, measurable targets for our sustainable food project.

activities.title: Co-constructing Measurable Project Criteria
activities.teacherDoes: Guide the class in drafting measurable criteria across three core domains: Nutritional Profile, Sensory & Aesthetic Quality, and Environmental Sustainability. Model converting the broad goal 'use local Yeppoon ingredients' into 'At least 70% of produce by weight sourced within 100km of Yeppoon, verified via supplier invoice'. Write the co-constructed examples explicitly on the board.
activities.studentsDo: Work with the teacher to formulate and record three distinct, measurable criteria statements into their workbook sections.
activities.visibleInstructions: Record the class-refined criteria for success into the three domains in your workbook. Ensure every statement includes an explicit numerical target or standard.
activities.questioning: How does defining a percentage of local produce make our sustainability claim verifiable? Expected: It allows an evaluator to audit ingredient weights and receipts rather than relying on an unsubstantiated claim. Why is it important to have criteria across multiple domains rather than just nutritional ones? Expected: A dish could be nutritionally perfect but commercially fail if it lacks sensory appeal or violates cost/sustainability constraints.
activities.scaffolding: Formula for Measurable Criteria: [Subject] + [Must achieve specific standard/value] + [As measured by verification method]. Domains to cover: 1. Nutritional Profile, 2. Sensory & Aesthetic Quality, 3. Environmental Sustainability.

activities.teacherDoes: Circulate the room, monitoring students as they draft four project-specific criteria for their chosen food trend design brief. expected: Students identify a quantitative metric such as cost per portion (<$5.00 via costing sheet) or cooking time (<15 mins via timer).

activities.title: Modelling Constructive Criteria Critique
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly demonstrate how to critique and upgrade weak criteria using the QCAA standards. Project two weak criteria: 'The dish must look modern and nice' and 'It should not cost too much to produce'. Model the rewrite process on the board: transforming 'modern and nice' into 'Plated using minimalist circular geometry with two contrasting sauces, evaluated at ≥4/5 on a presentation rubric', and 'not cost too much' into 'Total wholesale ingredient cost per portion must not exceed $4.20 AUD'.
activities.studentsDo: Transcribe the modeled improvements into the workbook and rewrite the weak criteria using the modeled protocol to make them actionable, precise, and measurable.
activities.visibleInstructions: Follow the teacher's critique model. Rewrite the weak criteria in your workbook to make them actionable, precise, and measurable.
activities.questioning:
q: Why does replacing 'cost too much' with '$4.20 AUD' protect a food designer during product evaluation?
Expected: A precise dollar threshold provides an objective pass/fail benchmark, preventing subjective disputes about what constitutes 'expensive'.
q: What happens if a design criterion is too restrictive?
Expected: It can stifle creative ideation during concept development by eliminating viable alternative solutions.
activities.scaffolding: Upgrade Formula: Remove subjective adjectives ('nice', 'fast', 'green') -> Insert verifiable metrics ('≥ 4/5 rating', '≤ 12 mins', '≥ 80% local ingredients').
activities.eLearning: Laptops open for assessment rubric reference only; direct teacher modelling on front projector.

activities.title: Peer Review Workshop
activities.teacherDoes: Facilitate a structured peer review workshop using explicit QCAA assessment standards. Model how to complete the Peer Review Matrix by assigning an objective score (1 to 3) and providing one actionable, constructive sentence starter. For example, demonstrate how to turn vague feedback ('make it cheaper') into an actionable instruction ('Add a specific cost ceiling of $5.00 per serve'). Circulate the room to ensure students provide rigorous, criteria-aligned feedback rather than surface-level praise.
activities.studentsDo: Conduct a formal peer audit of your partner's design brief and criteria for success. Complete the 3-indicator evaluation table in your workbook, providing a rating and a specific recommendation for improvement based on QCAA standards.

activities.questioning:
question: What makes an improvement suggestion 'actionable'?
expected: It provides a specific wording change, metric, or boundary rather than general advice like 'make it better'.
question: How does your partner's draft account for environmental sustainability or design constraints?
expected: By specifying waste reduction targets, packaging parameters, or local procurement percentages.
activities.scaffolding: Peer Review Prompts: 'To make this quantitative, add a measurement unit such as...', 'Your target audience description would be stronger if you specified their...', 'This constraint is currently too vague; define the exact limit for...'

activities.title: Vocabulary: Divergent vs. Convergent Ideation
activities.teacherDoes: Display the vocabulary matching table on the main screen. Explicitly teach the distinction between divergent thinking (expansive generation of multiple options without immediate critique) and convergent thinking (analytical filtering and synthesising to choose a viable design). Model using a culinary scenario: divergent ideation lists diverse alternative proteins (e.g. macroalgae, black soldier fly flour, pulses), while convergent ideation filters these against client acceptability, kitchen safety, and prep time constraints.
activities.studentsDo: In your workbook, match each of the three terms in column 1 to its correct definition from the bank by writing the matching letter (A, B, or C) in the Match column.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match each ideation term to its correct definition in your workbook table using the definition bank.
activities.questioning:
question: Why is divergent thinking essential before convergent selection in culinary design?
Expected: It prevents designers from fixing on an obvious or uninspired first idea, expanding creative flavour and technique possibilities.
question: What occurs if a team evaluates ideas too early during divergent thinking?
Expected: Premature critique stifles risk-taking and stops novel or unconventional concepts from emerging.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
1. Divergent Thinking: The cognitive process of generating a broad range of creative, open-ended solutions and alternative concepts without immediate critique.
2. Convergent Thinking: The cognitive process of analysing, filtering, and combining ideas to systematically select the single most viable design solution.
3. Trend Driver: A persistent underlying shift in consumer behaviour, societal needs, or environmental conditions that influences future product innovation.
activities.eLearning: Project definitions on screen. Check student engagement from the back of the room as workbooks are completed.
activities.transition: Now that we have established our core ideation terminology, we will examine how to deconstruct and structure these ideas into a culinary concept map.

activities.title: Guided Notes: Structured Mind Mapping for Meals
activities.teacherDoes: Model constructing a structured food ideation map on the whiteboard. Place the trend driver 'Hyper-Local Sustainability' at the centre. Construct three primary category branches: 'Locally Sourced Ingredients', 'Culinary Preparation Techniques', and 'Sensory & Visual Appeal'. Model populating secondary nodes using regional examples such as Keppel Bay seafood and seasonal Central Queensland produce. Think aloud to demonstrate how each ingredient or technique branch directly serves the central trend.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the whiteboard demonstration and complete the cloze passage in your workbook by inserting the missing terms from the word bank to define the structure of a culinary mind map.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the cloze passage in your workbook by writing the correct terms from the word bank into blanks 1 through 6.
activities.questioning:
question: Why must the central node remain the food trend driver rather than a specific dish?
Expected: Anchoring to the trend driver ensures all divergent branches remain aligned to the core brief rather than limiting thinking to one predetermined recipe.
question: Why should culinary techniques be mapped separately from raw ingredients?
Expected: The preparation technique dictates texture, thermal stability, and presentation, which transforms raw ingredients into an innovative dish.
activities.scaffolding:
Structure Guide:
- Central Node: Chosen Trend Driver (e.g. Sustainability, Functional Health, Cultural Fusion).
- Primary Branches: Ingredients, Culinary Techniques, Aesthetic Presentation.
- Secondary Nodes: Specific food items, cooking methods (e.g. sous-vide, fermentation), plating elements.

activities.title: I Do: Modelling Visual Plating & Callout Annotation
activities.teacherDoes: Project a photograph of a plated dining dish from Keppel Bay Marina dining gallery. Model using visual communication principles to deconstruct the presentation. Think aloud: 'Look at how the vivid orange roasted pumpkin puree directly contrasts the dark charcoal slate plate. That complementary colour scheme creates immediate visual pull. Notice how the hero barramundi fillet is positioned off-centre using the rule of thirds, creating dynamic asymmetrical balance.' Demonstrate drawing clean callout lines to the margins and writing precise, technical justifications.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the teacher modelling on the board. In your workbook annotate figure activity, use the numbered callouts (1–4) to label and explain the four key plating zones: Colour Contrast, Focal Point, Textural Variation/Height, and Negative Space.
activities.visibleInstructions: Examine the projected Keppel Bay Marina plated dish. On your workbook diagram, match callouts 1 to 4 to the correct plating zones and complete the written explanations.
activities.questioning:
q: Why is colour contrast particularly vital for culinary concepts presented on digital screens or in VR?
Expected: Digital screens compress subtle gradations, so high contrast is essential to make textures look appetizing and three-dimensional.
q: How does intentional negative space around the plate rim impact the diner's focus?
Expected: It removes visual clutter and directs the gaze inward toward the central culinary narrative.
activities.scaffolding:
Plating Principles:
1. Balance: Visual weight distribution (symmetrical = formal/stable; asymmetrical = dynamic/modern).
2. Contrast: Opposing visual properties (light vs dark, smooth purees vs crunchy tuiles).
3. Focal Point: The primary hero element where the eye lands first.
4. Negative Space: Intentional empty surface area that frames the dish.
activities.eLearning: Project Keppel Bay Marina food styling photography via the website stimulus (https://www.keppelbaymarina.com.au/). Ensure laptops remain closed during explicit modelling.
activities.transition: Now that we have analysed a professional plated dish, we will work together to critique and rectify a poorly composed culinary presentation.

activities.title: We Do: Co-constructing a Plating Critique
activities.teacherDoes: Display an image of an unrefined dish (e.g. monochromatic beige stew, no vertical elevation, overcrowded edges). Guide the class through a systematic critique audit. Prompt students to identify the specific visual defect, name the principle violated, and propose a concrete culinary design solution. Model the first row on the board: 'Monochromatic colour scheme | Colour Theory / Contrast | Introduce a contrasting vibrant sauce swipe (e.g. beetroot reduction or parsley oil)'.
activities.studentsDo: Collaborate with the teacher and peers to analyse the unrefined dish. Record the three agreed defects, the violated visual communication principles, and the proposed design fixes into your workbook table.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the 3-row audit table in your workbook. For each row, record the identified design defect, the design principle violated, and your proposed culinary fix.
activities.questioning: What is the primary visual risk of serving a dish with a monochromatic colour palette? Expected: It appears flat, unappetising, and visually indistinguishable, diminishing perceived flavour complexity. How can vertical height be incorporated without compromising the structural stability of the dish? Expected: By layering foundational starches, stacking the hero protein, or using crisp structural garnishes like tuiles or dehydrated crisps.
activities.scaffolding:
Audit Framework:
- Defect 1: Monochromatic / low contrast -> Principle: Colour Theory -> Fix: Vibrant emulsion, herb oil, or microgreens.
- Defect 2: Flat two-dimensional spread -> Principle: Balance & Proportion / Height -> Fix: Layered stacking, vegetable ribbons, crisp garnishes.
- Defect 3: Overcrowded rim -> Principle: Focal Point & Negative Space -> Fix: Tighten plating radius, retain 25-30% rim space.
activities.eLearning: Project the critique audit table on the whiteboard, recording student contributions in real time.
activities.transition: Now that you have audited and rectified these design flaws, apply these principles to independently sketch your own concept dish.

Don the headset and model selecting food assets from the virtual pantry, applying scale transforms to match real-world plating proportions, and adjusting placement along the Z-axis (height). Remove the headset and model transitioning to the design wireframe template. Explain: 'A digital wireframe is the visual architecture for your interactive recipe card. activities.questioning:
q: Why must we establish 3D scale in VR rather than relying solely on 2D sketch proportions?
Expected: A 2D sketch can conceal spatial collisions and unrealistic portion sizes that become immediately apparent when viewing depth in 3D VR.
q: What is the functional role of the primary Call-to-Action button on a digital recipe card?
Expected: It directs the user to commit to a decisive next step, such as starting the guided cook or saving the plating assembly.

activities.title: Vocabulary: Evaluation Terminology
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the three core pillars of evaluating design proposals: viability, feasibility, and desirability. Model how to define these terms using the whiteboard, drawing clear links to the 'Food Trends' design criteria. Emphasise how each term relates to QCAA Design Technologies evaluation standards: 'Feasibility relates to tools and workflow skills, viability relates to economic and environmental sustainability, and desirability relates to user trend appeal.' Direct students to match the terms to definitions using the provided bank.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the matching task in the workbook by writing the matching definition letter next to each locked evaluation term from the provided bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Match the 3 key evaluation terms (Feasibility, Viability, Desirability) with their correct definitions in your workbook table using the definition bank.
activities.questioning:
Why must a designed food solution achieve both feasibility and viability to be considered successful? Expected: Feasibility ensures it can be practically prepared with available kitchen tools and skills, while viability ensures it remains sustainable and economically realistic to produce over time.
How does market desirability influence the weighting of criteria in food design? Expected: If a dish meets all technical and sustainability criteria but lacks sensory or cultural appeal, target consumers will reject the product.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions in bank:
- Feasibility: The degree to which a food design can be practically executed given available culinary tools, technical skills, and kitchen preparation time.
- Viability: The capacity of a food design to operate successfully over time, considering economic cost, ethical sourcing, and environmental sustainability.
- Desirability: The degree to which a food design meets target audience preferences, contemporary trend drivers, and sensory appeal.
activities.eLearning: Project the vocabulary table on the whiteboard. Monitor workbook completion from the rear of the room.
activities.transition: Now that we have defined these evaluation principles, we will examine how to apply them systematically using a weighted decision matrix.

activities.title: Guided Notes: Weighted Decision-Matrix Modeling
activities.teacherDoes: Model how a Weighted Decision Matrix operates by demonstrating a live worked example comparing two exemplar dishes (e.g. locally sourced barramundi taco vs. broad-acre beef slider). Model how each raw score (1 to 5) is multiplied by criteria weight (e.g. Sustainability x3 = 15) and summed to determine the preferred concept. Emphasise that criteria weighting prevents subjective bias by enforcing objective measurement against the Criteria for Success.

activities.questioning:
question: Why do designers apply numerical weights to criteria rather than using a simple unweighted tally?
expected: Because some design factors, such as environmental sustainability or client constraints, carry higher priority than secondary factors like plating complexity.
question: What should a designer do if two divergent concepts finish with almost identical weighted totals?
expected: Re-examine the highest-weighted criteria scores or explore synthesising the strongest elements of both concepts.
activities.scaffolding:

Criteria weighting formula: Raw Score (1–5) × Criteria Weight = Weighted Score.

activities.title: Key Principles of Food Visual Communication
activities.teacherDoes: Explicitly teach the four core visual communication principles in culinary design: Balance (distribution of visual weight), Contrast (juxtaposition of textures, colours, and elevations), Scale (proportional relationships between food items and the plate), and Layout (deliberate arrangement using negative space and focal points). Expected: Asymmetrical balance creates dynamic visual flow and a contemporary aesthetic without appearing rigid or artificial.
What visual design issue occurs if negative space is ignored when plating a dish?
Expected: The plate becomes overcrowded and visually chaotic, obscuring the primary focal point and distinct meal components.
activities.scaffolding:
Definitions:
Balance: The deliberate distribution of visual weight across a plate (symmetrical or asymmetrical).
Contrast: The juxtaposition of opposing elements such as textures, heights, and colours.
Scale: The proportional size relationship between food components and tableware.
Layout: The structured placement of elements using focal points and negative space.

activities.title: Modelling Food Texture Rendering Techniques
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the three essential graphical rendering techniques for food materials on the document camera: 1. Glossy Glaze (leaving stark white unshaded highlights on convex curves to indicate moisture/reflectivity), 2. Crisp/Charred Crust (using dense stippling and short cross-hatching to represent rough texture), and 3. Smooth Viscous Puree (applying seamless circular gradient blending with no hard pencil lines). Emphasise that accurate rendering allows stakeholders to interpret mouthfeel before physical or VR production. Model the annotation syntax on the whiteboard using QCAA visual communication terminology.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the rendering demonstration, then complete the matrix in your workbook by matching target food textures to their graphical rendering technique and execution method.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the food texture rendering matrix in your workbook by matching the texture to its rendering technique and execution description.
activities.questioning:
How does leaving unshaded paper highlights communicate material properties on a food drawing?
Expected: It simulates specular reflection, indicating a liquid, glazed, or moist surface finish.
Why is stippling more effective than smooth shading for communicating a pan-seared crust?
Expected: Stippling produces irregular point variations that mimic the coarse, crunchy surface of seared proteins or toasted crumb.
activities.scaffolding:
Rendering Techniques:
- Glossy/Moist: Leave clean white paper highlights along curves to denote light reflection and moisture.
- Crisp/Rough: Apply stippling and fine cross-hatching to depict uneven surfaces and cellular crunch.
- Smooth/Pureed: Use continuous circular blending and smooth tone gradients to communicate uniform viscosity.
activities.eLearning: Ensure visualiser/document camera is focused clearly on the rendering demonstration paper.
activities.transition: Now that we have reviewed material rendering techniques, let's refine and polish our technical annotations using formal QCAA terminology.

activities.teacherDoes: The teacher models how to boot up the VR headset, configure screen recording parameters, test audio/visual frame rates, and verify the recording boundary before filming. Deliver this script: 'Watch as I lock the capture settings to 1080p at 60fps and verify my audio levels. activities.questioning:
Why is it critical to set capture quality to 60fps instead of 30fps for a fast-moving physical simulation like chopping in VR? Expected: Higher frame rates ensure rapid knife movements and digital tool interactions are rendered smoothly without motion blur during assessment review.
Where should the virtual camera be positioned to capture both the cooktop temperature dial and the pan contents simultaneously? Expected: Slightly above eye level, angled downwards at 45 degrees, keeping digital readouts and food texture changes in view.
activities.scaffolding: Recording check-list: 1. Audio active (mic enabled), 2. Resolution 1080p, 3. Framerate locked at 60fps, 4. Guardian boundary hidden in final output.

workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Critical evaluation: Systematically assessing the merit, success, or impact of a designed solution against fixed criteria. Iterative refinement: Making cyclic, evidence-based improvements to a prototype through progressive testing. Virtual prototyping: Using simulated digital environments to test form, workflow, and user experience prior to physical manufacture.

activities.title: Summative Design Evaluation Log
activities.teacherDoes: Model the construction of a summative evaluation paragraph using QCAA achievement standard language. Guide students to reference their Week 5 criteria for success, Week 8 annotated A3 page, and Week 9 VR production footage. For example, explicitly demonstrate how to link a design decision back to the original trend driver using evaluative terminology rather than descriptive recount.
activities.studentsDo: Draft comprehensive written evaluation responses across the three designated sections in your workbook, integrating specific evidence from your design journey.
activities.visibleInstructions: Complete the three structured evaluation sections in your workbook. Evaluate your trend alignment, analyse your VR workflow efficiency, and propose future technology innovations.
activities.questioning:
What concrete evidence from your VR simulation proves that your solution reduced food waste?
Expected: The ability to repeatedly calibrate ingredient portions and cooking temperatures virtually without consuming physical raw ingredients.
How will virtual reality technologies shape sustainable commercial food production in the next decade?
Expected: Commercial kitchens will use VR simulations for apprentice training, recipe prototyping, and ergonomic workflow optimisation to minimise resource use.
activities.scaffolding:
Evaluation writing guide:
1. Trend Alignment: Identify the trend driver, explain how the dish embodies it, and cite visual/nutritional evidence.
2. VR Workflow: Compare virtual prototyping efficiency against traditional physical trial cooks.
3. Future Innovations: Propose one emerging technology (e.g. AI nutrient formulation, haptic feedback) to enhance future iterations.
activities.eLearning: Students open their digital portfolios to reference their A3 design sheet and exported VR video clips.
activities.transition: Transition from evaluative writing to final digital asset verification and portfolio submission.

workbookSpec.prompt: Synthesise your design journey into a reflective evaluation addressing trend alignment, VR efficiency, and future industry implications.

3. Future Innovations: Integrating real-time AI nutrient calculators and haptic resistance into VR training simulations will further streamline commercial kitchen prototyping.

activities.title: Final Portfolio Verification and Submission
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through the final digital packaging protocols. Specify file naming conventions (e.g., Surname_Firstname_FutureFoodLab) and verify portal upload confirmations across all student workstations. Model the final file check by displaying the required directory structure on the main screen: 'Ensure your root folder contains exactly three validated assets: your MP4 showcase, your A3 PDF documentation, and your completed evaluation log.'
activities.studentsDo: Verify all digital files against the submission checklist in the workbook and complete the upload to the school assessment portal.
activities.visibleInstructions: Verify each component on your submission checklist, check file formats and naming conventions, and upload your complete project package to the portal.
activities.questioning:

Expected: It ensures clear attribution, systematic version control, and professional portfolio management.
What components comprise your complete summative assessment package?
Expected: The final MP4 VR cooking showcase, the A3 annotated design page PDF, and the completed reflective evaluation log.

weeks.title: Food Trends and VR Orientation
bullets: Explore global food trends like sustainability and health-conscious eating.
Learn the role of VR in food product design.
Master basic VR navigation, safety, and object interaction. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Food Safety and VR Kitchen Operations
bullets: Apply kitchen safety and hygiene fundamentals using HACCP principles.
Understand benefits of digital simulation for testing culinary skills.
Practise VR knife skills, heat control, and workflow safety. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Food Trend Drivers and Opportunities
bullets: Investigate social media and cultural impacts on food trends.
Analyse how food trends address future community needs.
Select a trend driver to inform your design brief. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Nutrition Science and Food Preservation
bullets: Examine macronutrients and their functional roles in meal design.
Investigate food spoilage, preservation techniques, and sustainable packaging.
Simulate preservation methods and variable changes in VR. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Design Briefs and Success Criteria
bullets: Deconstruct design briefs to identify client needs and constraints.
Establish measurable success criteria for nutritional and environmental impact.
Draft and peer-review your formal design brief. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Concept Ideation and VR Prototyping
bullets: Apply ideation techniques to explore initial meal concepts.
Apply visual design principles to food plating and layout.
Prototype three distinct meal concepts within the VR environment. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Refining Ideas and Technical Prototyping
bullets: Evaluate meal concepts against your established criteria for success.
Refine and merge ideas into a single dish design.
Test and validate recipe sequences inside the VR simulator. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Visual Communication and Final Concepts
bullets: Learn visual design principles for communicating food presentation.
Annotate design sketches to justify nutritional and sustainable choices.
Produce detailed rendered sketches of the final meal concept. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: VR Production and Pitch Preparation
bullets: Develop a pitch explaining trend alignment and design decisions.
Record and edit your final VR cooking sequence footage.
Rehearse presentation techniques for the final stakeholder pitch. (Content available on Teams)

weeks.title: Presentation, Evaluation and Reflection
bullets: Pitch your final VR cooking solution to the panel.
Evaluate your final product against established criteria for success.
Reflect on VR technology and future food sustainability. (Content available on Teams)
